problem: Social robot navigation research, despite three decades of work, still cannot deploy robots seamlessly in crowded pedestrian spaces. Earlier surveys (Kruse et al., Rios-Martinez et al., Rudenko et al.) cover sociology, perception or trajectory prediction separately. None critically diagnoses the fundamental limitations of planning formalisms, behavior models and evaluation practices (simulators, benchmarks, studies) together.
motivation: Robots that treat humans as non-reactive obstacles or plan with decoupled predictions cause failures in practice: the freezing robot problem, the 'reciprocal dance', and blocked human paths. Evaluation is dominated by homogeneous, cooperative simulators such as ORCA-driven crowds, which may give misleading conclusions. The authors want to follow up Kruse et al.'s call for a 'holistic theory of human-aware navigation' with formal definitions, a taxonomy and concrete research directions.
key_idea: Formalize social navigation as multi-agent path optimization with private costs plus a social cost that depends on predictions of others. Organize three decades of work into planning (decoupled vs. coupled prediction-planning), behavior (proxemics, intentions, formations) and evaluation (metrics, datasets, simulators, studies) challenges. Back the evaluation critique with a CrowdNav simulation study.
insight: Coupling prediction and planning is a core abstraction for social navigation, not a dense-crowd 'limit' phenomenon: even one nearby human raises effective density. Coupled formulations (interactive POMDPs, game theory, braids, joint inference, RL) are non-convex and NP-hard, and the safety/efficiency trade-off likely forms a Pareto front, so the objective is under-specified. The CrowdNav study shows two further problems. (1) In an ORCA crowd, a naive Simple Social Planner or even a Blind Planner reaches the goal much faster than an ORCA-driven robot, because it exploits ORCA agents' cooperativeness. (2) Learned policies (CADRL, SARL, RGL, MP-RGL) transfer poorly across crowd models: ORCA-trained policies are conservative, SFM-trained ones are faster but collide more yet generalize better to ORCA. SSP is roughly on par with the best RL method. Hence ORCA-only evaluation is uninformative and standardized, heterogeneous benchmarks are needed.
method: Formal problem definition: navigation as collision-free cost-minimizing path optimization in SE(2); social navigation as each agent minimizing c_i(τ_i) + λ_i c_i^s(τ_i, predicted τ_-i) under static-obstacle and inter-agent collision constraints, without access to others' costs/goals.

Planning taxonomy: decoupled prediction and planning (humans as dynamic non-responsive obstacles; interaction-agnostic uncertainty models; hand-engineered social objectives / IRL). Coupled prediction and planning, split into explicit (topological braids, game theory, Gestalt grouping, leader-follower) and implicit (IRL, interacting Gaussian processes, deep RL such as CADRL/SARL/GA3C, GAIL, intent-inference POMDP/MOMDP, LSTM/GAN/attention predictors).

Behavior taxonomy: proxemics (circular/egg/asymmetric/dynamic personal space, used as potential fields, hard boundaries or cost terms); intentions and legibility (legible, expressive motion); formations and social spaces (static F-formations, dynamic group detection/tracking, following/guiding, lane formation).

Evaluation review: metric catalogue (arrival rate, path length, collision rate, time to goal, path irregularity/efficiency, energy, ADE/FDE, DTW, comfort/social score, topological complexity). Statistics of ETH/Hotel/Univ/Zara1/Zara2 under these metrics (Table 2). Taxonomy of crowd models (microscopic/macroscopic/mesoscopic) and simulator software (PedSim, Menge, MengeROS, CrowdSim, UCrowds, SEAN-EP, etc.). Classification of real-world validation into demos, lab studies and field studies (Table 4).

CrowdNav simulation study: circular 3 m-radius workspace, 0.3 m disk agents, antipodal goals with goals re-sampled on arrival. Human crowds run ORCA or SFM; 8 density levels (5–49 humans), 100 random scenarios each. Robot planners: SSP, BP, ORCA, CADRL, SARL, RGL, MP-RGL, with RL policies trained by IL from an ORCA or SFM demonstrator then RL (10000 epochs, Adam, lr 0.001, γ=0.9). Holonomic robot with 80 discrete actions (5 speeds × 16 headings).

setting.backbone: n/a (survey); simulation study evaluates existing planners: SSP, Blind Planner, ORCA, CADRL, SARL, RGL, MP-RGL (small RL value networks trained by authors)
setting.training_data: For the simulation study only: RL baselines trained in CrowdNav via imitation learning from ORCA or SFM demonstrator then RL (10000 epochs)
setting.observation: full simulator state of robot and humans (positions/velocities) in CrowdNav
setting.action_space: holonomic, 80 discrete actions (5 exponentially spaced speeds in (0,1 m/s] × 16 headings)
setting.simulator: CrowdNav (ORCA and Social Force Model crowd environments)
setting.privileged: simulator provides exact states of all surrounding agents (no perception noise)

numbers_note: Survey paper; no own method is benchmarked on the canonical embodied-navigation benchmarks. The CrowdNav simulation study (time to goal and collisions vs. crowd density for SSP, BP, ORCA, CADRL, SARL, RGL, MP-RGL) is reported only in figures (Fig. 2, Fig. 3). The only numeric statements in text concern baselines (e.g., BP 'more than 70% of collision cases' in SFM; SSP fails above ~0.2 people/m²). Table 2 gives pedestrian-dataset statistics (ETH, HOTEL, UNIV, ZARA1, ZARA2), not method results.
results: Qualitative survey findings: coupled prediction and planning is essential but computationally intractable and non-convex, and behavior models lack principled knowledge. There is no standardized benchmark. The simulation study makes three points. In ORCA crowds, the naive SSP and even the Blind Planner reach the goal significantly faster than an ORCA-driven robot at all densities. In SFM crowds, SSP fails beyond ~0.2 people/m² and BP collides in >70% of cases. SSP is nearly identical to the best RL method (CADRL/SARL/RGL/MP-RGL), and these methods generalize poorly out of distribution: SFM-trained policies are faster but less safe, yet transfer better to ORCA.
limitations: Computational/algorithmic perspective only; robot design and perception pipelines are explicitly out of scope.
The empirical study is small and simulation-only (CrowdNav, holonomic robot, full-state observations), with results given only as plots, not tables.
Proposes a benchmark protocol and formal verification only as directions; no concrete benchmark or verified system is delivered.
